newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Cosatu warns on constitution court ruling.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Cosatu warns on constitution court ruling.

text.p: South Africa's biggest trade union federation warned employers on Friday against using the country's constitution-making process to hobble centralised bargaining or else face fierce labour resistance.

Commenting on the Constitutional Court's rejection of parts of the draft constitution, Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) general secretary Sam Shilowa said the federation was concerned at the ruling on collective bargaining.
"We are concerned at the implications of the Court's ruling in respect of collective bargaining rights for individual employers," Shilowa told reporters.
But the ruling not to entrench in the constitution employers' rights to lock out striking workers was a victory and justified Cosatu's struggle to exclude the clause, Shilowa said.
"The Court's findings that there is no need to entrench the right to lock-out in the Constitution is a great and historic victory for South Africa's working people," he said.
The Court found that the lock-out clause did not enjoy the status of a universally accepted fundamental human right.
But it also found that the proposed text of the constitution did not fully guarantee and protect an employer's right to bargain collectively.
While saying it respected the Court's ruling, by which the Constitutional Assembly has to comply, Cosatu urged that it be interpreted accurately and warned employers against opportunism.
"Nothing in the Court's judgment suggests that centralised bargaining is not permissable," Shilowa said.

"We warn employers that any attempt to use the opportunity of the constitution-making process to undermine hard-won centralised bargaining structures will be met with fierce resistance," Cosatu said in a statement.
Shilowa said that the ruling on collective bargaining had come as a surprise but that he believed the African National Congress-dominated government would interpret it correctly.
"They (ANC) have stood by us in the past and they will stand by us in this instance," Shilowa said.
"We call upon workers to remian vigilant to ensure that opportunists do not abuse the constitution-making process to undermine hard-won battles," Cosatu said.

The Constitutional Court President Arthur Chaskalson said on Friday that the 140-page constitution, hammered out by the country's first all-race parliament, failed in several respects to satisfy the minimum conditions hammered out in multi-party negotiations leading to democracy in 1994.
